propositions.text: This is a judicial review application of a visa officer's May 30, 2019 decision denying Applicant's permanent resident visa application.
propositions.quote: This is a judicial review application of the decision of a visa officer [Officer] of the Embassy of Canada in Poland, dated May 30, 2019, denying the Applicant’s application for a permanent resident visa in the Self-employed Persons class [Application] as the Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant had the ability or the intention to become self-employed in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of a visa officer's May 30, 2019 decision denying the Applicant's permanent resident visa application.

propositions.text: Applicant is Iranian, graduated from Iran’s University of Medical Sciences, and has a calligraphy diploma.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is an Iranian national. In addition to being a graduate of Iran’s University of Medical Sciences, the Applicant obtained a calligraphy diploma from the Persian Calligraphers Society.

propositions.text: Applicant filed application in May 2018 to be self-employed as an art producer in Iranian music.
propositions.quote: In May 2018, he filed his Application, wishing to be self-employed in Canada as an art producer in the field of Iranian music.

propositions.text: Applicant claimed about 20 years experience in Iranian music industry, including artistic director and producer at Avaye Barbad Institute from 2002 to 2008.
propositions.quote: When the Application was filed, the Applicant claimed he had about twenty years of experience in the Iranian music industry. In particular, he claimed that from 2002 to 2008 he worked as the artistic director and producer of the Avaye Barbad Institute [Institute], an Iranian corporate entity that produces, releases and distributes Iranian music all around the world.

propositions.text: Applicant designed more than 200 music album covers during his career.
propositions.quote: In the course of his career, the Applicant said he has designed more than 200 music album covers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is Iranian with medical and calligraphy diplomas, filed in 2018 to be self-employed in Iranian music, claiming 20 years experience including directing Avaye Barbad Institute and designing 200 album covers.

propositions.text: Since 2008, Applicant signed contracts with Institute to produce albums independently, published through Institute, and acquired all copyrights.
propositions.quote: Beginning in 2008, the Applicant states in his Application that he signed cooperation contracts with the Institute, allowing him to produce music albums independently, but they would be published and distributed through the Institute. He was also assigned all legal titles and copyrights in the past and future publications of the Institute.

propositions.text: In 2014, Applicant co-founded Barbad Records Inc. in Canada with two Canadian friends, aiming to be leading Persian, Arabic, Ebro music producer and distributor in North America and Europe.
propositions.quote: After having acquired all of the Institute’s copyrights and publications, the Applicant registered in Canada, in 2014, along with two Canadian friends, Barbad Records Inc. [Barbad Records], an artistic company aiming to become the leading Persian, Arabic and Ebro music artwork design service provider, producer and distributor for North America and Europe, while basing its operations in Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant owns 30% of Barbad Records and manages its overall direction and operations from Iran.
propositions.quote: According to the supporting documentation he filed along with the Application, the Applicant owns a thirty percent stake in Barbad Records and is in charge of the overall direction and operations of the company, which he ensures from abroad, as he still resides in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant signed contracts with Institute since 2008, acquired copyrights, co-founded Barbad Records in Canada in 2014, owns 30%, and manages it from Iran.

propositions.text: Since 2014, Barbad Records delivered over 500 music album titles globally and signed contract with American distributor The Orchard.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claimed that since 2014, Barbad Records has delivered more than 500 titles of music albums on digital music networks around the globe, has signed a contract with an American music distribution company – The Orchard – in order to expand the sale of its products and services in global markets,

propositions.text: Barbad Records registered trademark for Evercover app enabling users to create wallpapers from music album covers.
propositions.quote: and has registered a trademark for a mobile application – Evercover. That mobile application enables users of mobile and electronic devices to create wallpapers for their devices from music album covers that are available on a digital marketplace.

propositions.text: Barbad Records earned over $120,000 in 2017 and expected over $1 million in next three years.
propositions.quote: According to the Application, Barbad Records earned more than 120,000$ in revenues in 2017 and was expected to earn up to more than 1 million dollars in the following three years of its incorporation.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted bank deposit statements from Iran to show funds to invest in Barbad Records.
propositions.quote: Along with the Application, the Applicant submitted copies of deposit statements of his banking account in Iran to demonstrate that he had funds to invest in Barbad Records.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Barbad Records delivered 500+ albums globally, signed with The Orchard, registered Evercover app, earned $120,000 in 2017, expected $1 million, and Applicant submitted bank statements.

propositions.text: Officer denied Application on May 30, 2019, not satisfied Applicant had ability and intention to be self-employed in Canada.
propositions.quote: On May 30, 2019, the Officer denied the Application. In the rather laconic decision letter he sent to the Applicant, the Officer held that he was not satisfied that the Applicant had the ability and intention to become self-employed in Canada

propositions.text: Officer found Applicant did not meet definition of 'self-employed person' under subsection 88(1) of Immigration and Refugees Protection Regulations.
propositions.quote: and that he met, therefore, the definition of a “self-employed person” as set out in subsection 88(1) of the Immigration and Refugees Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [Regulations]. Because the Officer found the Applicant not to be a “self-employed person” within the meaning of that provision, no further assessment was required as per subsection 100(2) of the Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer denied the Application on May 30, 2019, finding Applicant lacked ability and intention to be self-employed and did not meet the definition under subsection 88(1).

propositions.text: Officer's GCMS notes indicated Applicant provided insufficient evidence of ability to be self-employed and Barbad Records' viability in Canada.
propositions.quote: In the notes he registered in the Global Case Management System [GCMS Notes], the Officer indicated that the Applicant provided insufficient evidence to demonstrate that he had the ability to be self-employed in Canada and that Barbad Records was a viable business for which there was room and need for in Canada.

propositions.text: Officer noted Barbad Records is a passive business run from overseas by Applicant.
propositions.quote: More particularly, the Officer noted that: Barbad Record is a passive business which the Applicant has been running or co-running from overseas;

propositions.text: Financial statements from 2014-2016 showed deficits and raised doubts about Barbad Records' viability.
propositions.quote: Barbad Records’ financial statements for the period between 2014 and 2016 showed a deficit in the company’s assets and raised doubt as to its viability;

propositions.text: Business plan provided only general Canadian industry info with limited relation to Applicant's proposed self-employment.
propositions.quote: Barbad Records’s business plan only provided general and statistical information about the industry in Canada and only provided limited information as to how this general information relates to the Applicant’s proposed self-employment;

propositions.text: Applicant had not made an exploratory visit to Canada, which Officer found unusual given co-ownership since 2014.
propositions.quote: Although such a visit was not required, the Applicant has not made an exploratory visit to Canada, which the Officer found somewhat unusual given that he has co-owned Barbad Records since 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer's GCMS notes found insufficient evidence of Applicant's ability and Barbad Records' viability, noting it is passive, had deficits, a general business plan, and no exploratory Canada visit.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer breached procedural fairness by not giving opportunity to address concerns before rejection.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the Officer breached the principles of procedural fairness by failing to provide him with an opportunity to address the Officer’s concerns prior to the rejection of the Application.

propositions.text: Applicant acknowledges no statutory right to interview but claims entitlement to fairness letter informing of concerns.
propositions.quote: Acknowledging that there is no statutory right to an interview for visa applicants, the Applicant submits that he was nevertheless entitled to be informed of the Officer’s concerns by way of a fairness letter.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer breached procedural fairness by not allowing response to concerns and claims entitlement to a fairness letter despite no interview right.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer erred by ignoring or unreasonably misconstruing relevant, substantial, probative evidence on intention and ability.
propositions.quote: He submits as well that the Officer committed a reviewable error in assessing his intention and ability to become a permanent resident of Canada under the Self-employed Persons class, by ignoring relevant, substantial and probative evidence or by unreasonably misconstruing the evidence before him.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer erred by ignoring or misconstruing relevant evidence on his intention and ability to be self-employed.

propositions.text: Applicant raises procedural fairness and reasonableness issues; procedural fairness reviewed on correctness standard, reasonableness on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is raising procedural fairness and reasonableness issues. It is not contested that the former is reviewable on a standard of correctness (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43) whereas the latter is reviewable on a standard of reasonableness (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 16-17 and 25 [Vavilov]; Rabbani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 257 at para 18-20).

propositions.text: Correctness standard attracts no deference; reasonableness standard attracts deference.
propositions.quote: It is trite law that the correctness standard does not attract any deference from the reviewing Court, but that the standard of reasonableness does.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant raises procedural fairness (correctness standard) and reasonableness (reasonableness standard) issues; correctness attracts no deference, reasonableness does.

propositions.text: Court is not satisfied procedural fairness duty was breached; little case law supports Applicant's contention for response opportunity when unaware of concerns.
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied that the duty of procedural fairness owed to the Applicant was breached in this case as I do not see much support in the case law for the Applicant’s contention that an opportunity to respond should be available to visa applicants whenever “they are unaware that the visa officer has any concerns about their applications” (Applicant’s Memorandum of Fact and Law at para 38).

paragraphs.summary: The court is not satisfied procedural fairness was breached; little case law supports Applicant's claim for response opportunity when unaware of concerns.

propositions.text: Duty of procedural fairness to visa applicants is limited and low on natural justice spectrum.
propositions.quote: As is well established, the duty of procedural fairness owed to visa applicants is limited and positions itself on the lower end of the spectrum of the protection contemplated by the principles of natural justice (Hamza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 264 at para 23; Tollerene v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 538 at para 15 [Tollerene]; Gur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1275 at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the duty of procedural fairness to visa applicants is limited and low on natural justice spectrum.

propositions.text: Visa applicants get response opportunity only if officer bases adverse conclusion on unknown info or concerns credibility/authenticity.
propositions.quote: This means that a visa applicant will generally only be offered the opportunity to respond to a potentially adverse conclusion where the visa officer may base said conclusion on information not known to the applicant or when the officer’s concern lies with the applicant’s credibility or the authenticity of documents he/she submitted in support of his/her application (Momeni v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 304 at para 24 [Momeni]; see also Tollerene at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa applicants get response opportunity only if officer bases adverse conclusion on unknown info or credibility/authenticity concerns.

propositions.text: Visa officer has no legal obligation to clarify deficient application, make applicant's case, inform applicant of concerns, or offer further response opportunities.
propositions.quote: Putting it differently, a visa officer has no legal obligation “to seek to clarify a deficient application, to reach out and make the applicant’s case, to apprise an applicant of concerns relating to whether the requirements set out in the legislation have been met, to provide the applicant with a running score at every step of the application process, or to offer further opportunities to respond to continuing concerns or deficiencies” (Lv v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 935 at para 23).

paragraphs.summary: The court states visa officers have no legal obligation to clarify applications, make applicant's case, inform of concerns, or offer further response chances.

propositions.text: Applicant did not establish exceptions apply: no evidence unknown to him or concerns about credibility/authenticity.
propositions.quote: Here, the Applicant has not established that neither exception to these principles applies. First, he has not pointed to any evidence considered by the Officer that was unknown to him. Second, he has not even raised that the Officer’s concerns lie with his credibility or the authenticity of documents he submitted in support of the Application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant did not establish exceptions for response opportunity: no unknown evidence or credibility/authenticity concerns.

propositions.text: Applicant relies on Mohitian v Canada to argue procedural fairness breach.
propositions.quote: Reliance on Mohitian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1393, does not advance the Applicant’s argument either.

propositions.text: In Mohitian, visa officer's decision was unreasonable due to contradictory decision letter and GCMS notes, making decision unintelligible.
propositions.quote: In that case, the Court found that the decision of the visa officer was unreasonable because the decision letter and the GCMS notes were fundamentally contradictory, which made the decision unintelligible and, accordingly, unreasonable.

propositions.text: Mohitian's visa application was in abeyance for over seven years; weeks before denial, applicant was asked for updated forms and documents but not business plan.
propositions.quote: It appears that the visa application in that case had been in abeyance for more than seven years and that only a few weeks prior to the visa officer’s decision denying the visa application, the applicant was requested to provide updated forms and documentation, with a detailed two-pages checklist as to what forms and other documentation he needed to submit. However, there was no requirement, in said checklist, to provide a business plan.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant relies on Mohitian v Canada; court finds Mohitian decision unreasonable due to contradictory notes and long delay with no business plan request.

propositions.text: Visa officer in Mohitian expressed concerns about business plan realism without prior input from applicant, leading to unfairness finding.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, the visa officer expressed concerns in his decision as to whether the applicant’s business plan was realistic. That resulted in the Court finding that it was not fair in these circumstances for the visa officer not to have alerted the applicant of his concerns regarding his business plan.

paragraphs.summary: Court found Mohitian visa officer unfairly did not alert applicant of business plan concerns before decision.

propositions.text: Mohitian's circumstances—7+ years processing, prompt info request excluding business plan, and inference business plan was not important—were key to fairness breach finding.
propositions.quote: I believe that the particular circumstances of that case namely the fact that it took more than seven years to process the applicant’s visa application, the promptness in dealing with said application after the applicant was requested to provide a detailed list of updated information that did not include the provision of a business plan or updated business pan and the resulting reasonable inference that the provision of such a document was not important or that the one provided by the applicant did not raise any issues after all – played key roles in the Court’s finding that this amounted to a breach of the duty of procedural fairness owed to the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Mohitian's long delay and info request excluding business plan were key to procedural fairness breach finding.

propositions.text: No similar circumstances exist in this case to support procedural fairness breach.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that there are no such circumstances in the case at bar.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no similar circumstances here to support procedural fairness breach.

propositions.text: Court is not prepared to conclude Officer's decision is reasonable.
propositions.quote: That being said, I am not prepared, however, to conclude that the Officer’s decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: Court is not prepared to conclude Officer's decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Legal and policy framework for Self-employed Persons class described in Momeni case.
propositions.quote: The legal and policy framework that applies to visa applications made under the Self‑employed Persons class was described as follows in Momeni: [5] Subsection 12(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], provides that foreign nationals may be selected for permanent residence as members of the economic class on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada. [6] Division 2 of the [Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (IRPR)] establishes classes of business immigrants. One of those classes is the Self-employed Person Class. Section 100 of the IRPR provides that based on ability to become economically established in Canada, a foreign national who is self-employed within the meaning of the IRPR may become a permanent resident. Section 100 further states that where a foreign national who applies under the Self-employed Person Class is not a self-employed person within the meaning of the IRPR, the application shall be refused: 100 (1) For the purposes of subsection 12(2) of the Act, the self-employed persons class is hereby prescribed as a class of persons who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada and who are self-employed persons within the meaning of subsection 88(1). 100 (1) Pour l’application du paragraphe 12(2) de la Loi, la catégorie des travailleurs autonomes est une catégorie réglementaire de personnes qui peuvent devenir résidents permanents du fait de leur capacité à réussir leur établissement économique au Canada et qui sont des travailleurs autonomes au sens du paragraphe 88(1). (2) If a foreign national who applies as a member of the self-employed persons class is not a self-employed person within the meaning of subsection 88(1), the application shall be refused and no further assessment is required. (2) Si le demandeur au titre de la catégorie des travailleurs autonomes n’est pas un travailleur autonome au sens du paragraphe 88(1), l’agent met fin à l’examen de la demande et la rejette. [7] The IRPR defines a “self-employed person” at subsection 88(1) (emphasis added): self-employed person means a foreign national who has relevant experience and has the intention and ability to be self-employed in Canada and to make a significant contribution to specified economic activities in Canada travailleur autonome Étranger qui a l’expérience utile et qui a l’intention et est en mesure de créer son propre emploi au Canada et de contribuer de manière importante à des activités économiques déterminées au Canada. [8] “Relevant experience” is also defined at subsection 88(1). The relevant experience requirements differ depending on whether the self-employed person’s experience has been obtained in the field of (i) cultural activities, (ii) athletics, or (iii) the purchase and management of a farm. Mr. Momeni’s claimed experience is in the field of cultural activities: relevant experience, in respect of expér

paragraphs.summary: Court describes legal and policy framework for Self-employed Persons class as in Momeni, including IRPA and IRPR provisions and definition of self-employed person.

propositions.text: Definition of 'self-employed person' involves 'intention' and 'ability' per subsection 88(1) of the Regulations
propositions.quote: the concepts of “intention” and “ability” that are found in the definition of “self-employed person” set out in subsection 88(1) of the Regulations (Wei v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 982 [Wei])

propositions.text: Permanent residency is a reward if success results from self-employment project
propositions.quote: permanent residency status is necessary for the success of the project, not that the project can succeed otherwise, but that the [a]pplicant should be rewarded with permanent residency if success results

propositions.text: Goal is applicant's significant contribution to specified economic activity in Canada
propositions.quote: Applicant be self-employed in Canada for the purpose of significantly contributing to a specified economic activity

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker explained 'self-employed person' means intention and ability per subsection 88(1), with permanent residency as a reward for success and significant economic contribution.

propositions.text: Applicant must extensively plan and detail means of executing proposed self-employment activities in Canada
propositions.quote: a permanent resident visa applicant must demonstrate that he/she has extensively planned and detailed the means of execution of his proposed activities in Canada as a self-employed person

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker held applicants must extensively plan and detail execution means for self-employment in Canada.

propositions.text: Intention is a mental attribute found by examining past external conduct evidence
propositions.quote: intention to be self-employed... can only be found as a fact by the examination of past external conduct evidence broadly defined

propositions.text: Intention to fulfill future commitment depends on evidence of significant past commitment enabling the project
propositions.quote: intention to fulfill a future commitment depends on evidence of a significant past commitment that goes a long way in enabling the project

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker held intention is found by examining past conduct and depends on evidence of significant past commitment.

propositions.text: Applicants must demonstrate thoroughly conceived projects and concrete steps for successful economic activity
propositions.quote: a demonstration that the projects have been thoroughly conceived and concrete steps taken to ensure the implementation that will result in a successful economic activity

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker emphasized applicants must show thoroughly conceived projects and concrete steps for success.

propositions.text: Visa officers have high discretion and deference in permanent residence visa applications
propositions.quote: visa officers considering permanent residence visa applications enjoy a high degree of discretion and are entitled to a considerable degree of deference

propositions.text: Discretion of visa officers is not absolute
propositions.quote: that discretion... is not absolute

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states visa officers have high but not absolute discretion in permanent residence visa applications.

propositions.text: Administrative decision makers have specialized expertise on questions before them
propositions.quote: administrative decision makers are understood to possess specialized expertise on all questions that come before them

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires focusing on the decision made and justification offered, not court's own conclusion
propositions.quote: focus on the decision the administrative decision maker actually made, including the justification offered for it, and not on the conclusion the court itself would have reached

propositions.text: Reasonableness review is deferential and starts with judicial restraint
propositions.quote: reasonableness review finds its starting point in judicial restraint and has always been, and is still, considered as a deferential standard of review

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states administrative decision makers have expertise; reasonableness review focuses on their decision and justification with judicial restraint.

propositions.text: Reasons for decision are primary mechanism to show reasonableness to parties and courts
propositions.quote: reasons for decision are the primary mechanism by which administrative decision makers show that their decisions are reasonable

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is based on internally coherent and rational chain of analysis
propositions.quote: a reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis

propositions.text: Reasonable decision must exhibit justification, intelligibility, transparency and be justified by relevant facts and law
propositions.quote: a reasonable decision is one that exhibit[s] the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency and which is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints

propositions.text: Reasons need not be perfect but mere repetition of statutory language and peremptory conclusions rarely assist courts
propositions.quote: Reasons that simply repeat statutory language, summarize arguments made, and then state a peremptory conclusion will rarely assist a reviewing court

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states reasons must show reasonableness with coherent analysis, justification, and transparency; mere repetition and peremptory conclusions are insufficient.

propositions.text: Reviewing court must not provide reasons not given or speculate on decision-maker's thoughts when reasons are silent
propositions.quote: reviewing court must guard against providing reasons that were not given by the administrative decision-maker or from guessing what findings might have been made

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states courts must not supply reasons or speculate when decision-maker's reasons are silent.

propositions.text: Court may intervene if decision-maker fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for evidence
propositions.quote: a reviewing court will be entitled to intervene when the decision-maker has fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states court may intervene if decision-maker fundamentally misapprehended or ignored evidence.

propositions.text: Officer's decision shows shortcomings justifying court intervention
propositions.quote: the Officer’s decision shows shortcomings justifying the Court’s intervention

propositions.text: Officer failed to explain with justification, intelligibility and transparency why Applicant's ability, means and intention were reasonably doubted
propositions.quote: failed to explain with the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency, how and why the Applicant’s ability, means and intention... could reasonably be doubted

propositions.text: Impugned decision lacks justification, intelligibility and transparency related to facts and law constraining Officer
propositions.quote: the impugned decision fails to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency in relation to the facts and law that constrained the Officer decision-making process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's decision lacks justification and transparency, justifying intervention.

propositions.text: Officer found Barbad Records was a 'passive business' run from overseas but did not explain 'passive business' meaning
propositions.quote: he found that Barbad Records was “a passive business” which the Applicant had been running or co-running from overseas. However, the Officer did not explain what he meant by “a passive business”

propositions.text: Evidence suggests Barbad Records had steady activities ensuring viability and success of self-employment project
propositions.quote: evidence provided by the Applicant... suggest a steady flow of activities aimed at ensuring the viability and the success of the self-employment project behind Barbad Records

propositions.text: Barbad Records active in Canada since 2014, benefited from copyrights, generated revenues, signed contract with American distributor
propositions.quote: Barbad Records has been active in Canada since it was incorporated in 2014; It has benefited from the copyrights... It has generated revenues; It has signed a contract with an important American music distribution company

propositions.text: Barbad Records registered Canadian trademark, developed mobile app, has Canadian shareholders and officers
propositions.quote: It has registered a Canadian trademark and developed a mobile application... It has Canadian shareholders and officers

propositions.text: Applicant has close to $400,000 funds to invest and plans to invest $150,000 upon settling in Canada
propositions.quote: The Applicant – has close to 400,000$ of funds available to invest... will invest... 150,000$ of these funds as soon as he is allowed to settle in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's 'passive business' finding unexplained and inconsistent with evidence of Barbad Records' active operations and Applicant's funds.

propositions.text: Officer found Barbad Records' 2014-2016 financial statements showed asset deficits and doubted viability
propositions.quote: Barbad Records’ financial statements for the period between 2014 and 2016 showed a deficit in the company’s assets and raised doubt as to its viability

propositions.text: Officer did not mention Applicant's available funds, revenues generated, or growth potential in GCMS notes
propositions.quote: no mention in the Officer’s GCMS notes about the funds that the Applicant has available... or of the revenues Barbad Records has generated... or of its potential for growth

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer doubted viability based on deficits but ignored Applicant's funds, revenues, and growth potential.

propositions.text: Officer criticized business plan as limited and theoretical without sufficient explanation
propositions.quote: Officer was critical of Barbad Records’ business plan, which he found to provide limited, theoretical information

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion is peremptory and unsupported by whole evidence on Applicant's ability and execution means
propositions.quote: Without more, this amounts to a peremptory conclusion when considered in light of the whole evidence

propositions.text: Such peremptory conclusions do not meet justification test per Vavilov para 102
propositions.quote: This does not meet the justification test, as set out in Vavilov at para 102

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's criticism of the business plan is peremptory and unjustified under Vavilov.

propositions.text: Officer noted Applicant made no exploratory visit to Canada since incorporation of Barbad Records
propositions.quote: Applicant had made no exploratory visit to Canada since the incorporation of Barbad Records

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged visit not required but found lack of visit 'unusual' given co-ownership since 2014
propositions.quote: he acknowledged that such a visit was not a requirement... he found that “unusual” given that the Applicant has co-owned Barbad Records since 2014

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer noted no exploratory visit and found it unusual despite no requirement.

propositions.text: Applicant's lack of travel to Canada is irrelevant to Self-employed Persons visa analysis
propositions.quote: a visa applicant has never travelled to Canada is indeed irrelevant to the analysis of a visa application in the Self-employed Persons class

propositions.text: Unknown what weight Officer gave to lack of visit; court must not speculate
propositions.quote: What we do not know here is the weight the Officer accorded to that finding... it is not for the Court to speculate on that

propositions.text: Finding alone constitutes a reviewable error
propositions.quote: In and of itself, this finding constitutes, for that reason, a reviewable error

paragraphs.summary: The court finds lack of travel irrelevant, unknown weight given by Officer, and that this alone is a reviewable error.

propositions.text: Respondent counsel raised alleged inconsistencies in Applicant's evidence to Officer
propositions.quote: counsel for the Respondent raised a number of what he considered to be inconsistencies in the evidence provided to the Officer by the Applicant

propositions.text: Officer did not address these inconsistencies; court will not consider them as it would supply reasons not given
propositions.quote: these inconsistencies were not addressed by the Officer in his decision and shall not be considered by the Court

propositions.text: Court must not provide reasons not given by Officer (Vavilov para 97)
propositions.quote: Respondent’s submissions on this point amounts to an invitation to provide reasons that were not given by the Officer

paragraphs.summary: Respondent alleges inconsistencies; court refuses to consider as Officer did not address them, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Officer's reasons do not allow court to understand decision or determine if outcome is acceptable
propositions.quote: reasons provided by the Officer do not allow the Court to understand... why the Officer made his decision and... whether the conclusion... falls within the range of acceptable outcomes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer's reasons insufficient to understand or assess decision's acceptability.

propositions.text: Vavilov affirms need to develop culture of justification in administrative decision making
propositions.quote: Vavilov affirms “the need to develop and strengthen a culture of justification in administrative decision making”

propositions.text: Court intervention warranted as Officer failed to justify doubts about Applicant's ability, means and intention
propositions.quote: this is a case where the Court’s intervention is warranted as the Officer failed to explain with the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency, how and why the Applicant’s ability, means and intention... could reasonably be doubted

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes intervention is warranted due to Officer's failure to justify doubts about Applicant's ability, means, and intention.

propositions.text: Judicial review application granted; Officer's decision set aside; matter remitted to different visa officer
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is granted; The decision of the Officer... is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different visa officer for redetermination

propositions.text: Applicant claimed costs but waived request at hearing
propositions.quote: Applicant claimed his costs. However, he waived this request at the hearing

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, sets aside Officer's decision, remits matter, and notes Applicant waived costs claim.
